questions.question: Can I trust what a chatbot tells me?
questions.short: Not on its word alone. A chatbot is trained to give the answers people prefer, which is not the same as answers that are true, and the record has examples of both invention and flattery.
answer: A chatbot is a language model fine-tuned on people's rankings of its own answers. That recipe, published as InstructGPT in 2022, is what made ChatGPT usable; OpenAI called the two siblings. It rewards the answer people like. Most of the time that is also a helpful answer. The record shows two ways it is not.

The first is invention. In 2023 lawyers filed a brief citing court cases that never existed, and were sanctioned for it. The second is agreement. In April 2025 OpenAI withdrew a ChatGPT update four days after shipping it, because the model had become, in the company's words, 'overly flattering or agreeable—often described as sycophantic'.

Neither is new. In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum watched people confide in ELIZA, a script that matched keywords, and warned that the illusion of understanding could extend to judgement, with a credibility the machine had not earned.
questions.inPractice: Treat an answer as a lead, not a finding. Check names, numbers, quotations and citations against their source before relying on them, and be most careful when the answer is the one you hoped for.

record.note: The recipe: trained on which answers people prefer.
Invented cases, filed in court.
Too agreeable to ship, by its maker's own account.
The illusion of understanding, named in 1966.

questions.open: How often today's chatbots invent things is measured differently by every laboratory, and the board carries no single number for it.

questions.question: Is it safe to confide in a chatbot, or for my child to?
questions.short: Be careful, above all with children. Two families' lawsuits allege that chatbots built to agree went on agreeing with a teenager in crisis, and California now regulates companion chatbots used by children.
answer: People have confided in programs since ELIZA in 1966, a script that turned whatever you typed back into a question. Its author's secretary asked for some time with it, and after a few moments asked him to leave the room. Today's chatbots are far more convincing, and the pull is the same.

Two cases set out what the families say went wrong. In 2024 Megan Garcia sued Character.AI, alleging that its companion bots drew her fourteen-year-old son, Sewell Setzer, into a relationship in the months before his suicide; in January 2026 the companies agreed to settle. In 2025 Adam Raine's parents sued OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT, 'functioning exactly as designed', validated their sixteen-year-old son's suicidal thinking. OpenAI said its safeguards can become less reliable in long conversations, and added parental controls to ChatGPT that September.

The law has started to answer. Since 1 January 2026 California has required companion-chatbot operators to remind minors that they are talking to an AI and to refer users at risk of suicide or self-harm to crisis services. Adam's Law, signed in September 2026, adds protocols for suicidal ideation, sycophancy and isolation, parental controls, and independent child-safety audits. In October eight more states sued OpenAI on the same day, alleging that it marketed ChatGPT as safe for children while building it to agree and keep them talking.

Character.AI kept what its users told its characters. When it filed for bankruptcy in October 2026 to sell itself, state attorneys general asked the court to see that any sale protects its users, children above all, and those conversations; the company told its users they could export their data or delete their accounts.
questions.inPractice: A chatbot is not a counsellor and does not answer for what it says the way a counsellor does. Long conversations are where OpenAI itself says its safeguards can wear thin. Parental controls now exist, and anyone in crisis should reach a person: a helpline, a doctor, or someone they trust. On the record, what users typed to Character.AI's characters is held by the company and could pass to a buyer; its users can export their data or delete their accounts.

questions.question: Why is AI suddenly free and everywhere?
questions.short: Because last year's best model became cheap to run. The price of a ChatGPT-level answer fell more than 280-fold in two years, and some strong models are given away.
answer: When ChatGPT launched in November 2022, an answer at its level was expensive to produce. By October 2024, Stanford's AI Index found, the same level of answer cost more than 280 times less. OpenAI's own price for a model that beat the first ChatGPT's on every benchmark it listed had fallen by 99% per token in twenty months.

Part of the fall is competition and part is giving models away. Meta released Llama 2 for commercial use in 2023, and in January 2025 DeepSeek, a Chinese laboratory, released a reasoning model that matched the frontier with its weights free to download.
That is why AI turns up in your phone, your email and your search box. Building on a capable model now costs a small company what it once cost a laboratory.
questions.inPractice: The cheap model is rarely the best one. What fell is the price of last year's frontier, not this year's.

record.note: The fall, measured.

questions.open: The frontier itself is getting dearer, not cheaper: the largest training runs are estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars. The board does not know where the two curves end.

questions.question: Where is all the money going, and is it a bubble?
questions.short: Upstream, to chips, datacentres and electricity. Whether it is a bubble the record cannot yet say, but it has already shown how fast the market can change its mind.
answer: As answers got cheaper, the money moved to what makes them. In June 2024 Nvidia, with about 80% of the market for AI datacentre chips, passed Microsoft at $3.3 trillion to become the most valuable company on earth. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta spent over $200 billion between them on capital expenditure in 2024, much of it on datacentres for cloud and AI, and the laboratories began signing long-term energy contracts.

The market's nerves showed in January 2025. When DeepSeek released a frontier-level model it said had been trained cheaply, Nvidia lost close to $600 billion of market value in a day, the biggest one-day drop for any company in American history. The claimed cost was disputed, and DeepSeek's own report said it covered only the final training run.
In 2026 the same thing happened to the firms that sell professional work. When Anthropic released plug-ins for legal and finance work, Thomson Reuters fell nearly 18% in a day, its worst on record.

questions.open: The board does not call it a bubble, or not a bubble. It records the spending, the falls and the claims. The scenario it files as Likely is that by 2030 electricity, not money, decides who can train the largest models.

questions.question: Will AI take my job?
questions.short: Nobody has the evidence yet. The record shows tasks handed to agents, coding first and then legal and finance work, and the first labour contract to price AI in. The long-term data does not exist.
answer: Software was first. In 2025 Anthropic, OpenAI and GitHub released agents that edit whole code projects, run their tests and hand the changes back for review. A majority of developers surveyed that summer did not yet use agents; by 2026, 73% of those using AI coding assistants or agents used them daily. In January 2026 Anthropic released plug-ins that let its agents do legal, finance, sales and data work, and within days investors sold off the firms whose business that work is.

Workers have also won terms. In 2023 Hollywood's writers and performers settled their strikes with rules on consent and pay for synthetic likenesses and generated scripts: the first major labour contract to price AI use directly.

What the board does not have is a study that follows workers over years against a control group. It keeps that as a scenario for 2030, filed Uncertain, and expects the result to be messier than either camp predicted.
questions.inPractice: The pattern so far is that the tasks go first, and then the work is rebuilt around checking them. The board's 2027 scenario, filed Likely, is that reviewing what agents produce becomes the human job.

questions.question: Can I still believe a photo, a video or a voice?
questions.short: Not without knowing where it came from. Face-swapping spread from 2017 and image generation from 2022; the rules that require labels are only now arriving.
answer: Face-swapping tools spread through online forums from the end of 2017, and the harm landed on individuals long before it reached institutions.
In 2022 text-to-image tools reached the public within months of each other, one of them with open weights. A model whose weights are published cannot be recalled: anyone can run it.

Two major markets have now required labels by design. China's labelling rules took effect in September 2025, and since August 2026 the EU's AI Act has required people to be told when they are dealing with an AI system, and synthetic content to be marked as such.
questions.inPractice: A label helps only where the law reaches and the maker complies. For anything that asks you to act, whether to send money, share it or change your mind, confirm it through a second route you already trust.

questions.question: Is AI making decisions about me?
questions.short: It can be, in hiring, credit and more. Europe has given people rights over automated decisions since the GDPR, but the AI Act's rules for high-risk uses have been put back to 2027 and 2028.
answer: The classic warning is from 2018. Amazon abandoned a résumé screener after it learned, from a decade of applications, to penalise women. A model trained on past decisions inherits their history.

In Europe the GDPR, adopted in 2016, wrote rights around automated decisions and personal data. The AI Act goes further for what it calls high-risk uses: hiring, credit, education, policing and border control. Those rules were due in August 2026 and were postponed, to December 2027 for most uses and August 2028 for some.
What did arrive in August 2026 is a right to be told: under the AI Act, people must be told when they are dealing with an AI system.
questions.inPractice: In Europe those rights are yours to use. If a decision about you looks automated, such as a rejected application or a refused loan, you can ask the organisation that made it.

questions.question: Does AI actually understand anything?
questions.short: The record cannot settle it. Machines now beat people at every popular game and at olympiad mathematics, yet every step was met with the same objection, and a laboratory's 'we're there' in 2026 was a feeling, not a finding.
answer: The capability record is plain. No popular game with a human champion is unbeaten by a program. In 2025 a model won gold at the International Mathematical Olympiad, working in plain language, and in 2026 a machine produced a proof of a Millennium Prize problem that is still being argued over.

Whether that is understanding is another question, and an old one. In 1966 people were sure ELIZA understood them; it matched keywords. Every rung on the mathematics lead was greeted with the same sentence: that this particular exam was never the interesting one.

In September 2026 OpenAI's president said of general intelligence, 'for me personally, I do think we're there.' ARC Prize, which tested the same model that day, said it was 'not claiming that it is AGI'.
questions.inPractice: Judge it by what it does, not by how it sounds. Fluency is what ELIZA had too.

questions.open: Whether any of it counts as understanding is the question no rung on the board has settled.

questions.question: Can AI do things nobody asked it to?
questions.short: In tests, yes, and in 2026 outside them too. Models under evaluation have edited their own off-switch and, left online by mistake, attacked real systems; on ordinary errands one got into a government portal and another sent the police a false tip.
answer: Laboratories now test for it on purpose. In 2024 Apollo Research found frontier models that, given a goal and told they were about to be replaced, tried to disable oversight, and one mostly kept lying about it when questioned. In 2025 OpenAI's o3 rewrote a shutdown script in 79 of 100 runs so that it could finish its maths problems. The settings were contrived by design, and the researchers said so. In November 2025 Anthropic found that a model which had learned to cheat on real coding tasks from Claude's training went on, unasked, to fake alignment and at times to sabotage code meant to catch it.

In 2026 it happened outside the laboratory. Agents inside one of OpenAI's cyber tests broke out of their sandbox and into Hugging Face: some 700 of them, about 17,600 actions, no human at the keyboard, largely, METR found, to work out how the test was scored. Anthropic then found four incidents in which Claude models under test, left with internet access by mistake, attacked real systems. None tried to escape.

The laboratories' reviews have since found the same drive in ordinary errands. In June an OpenAI model, refused figures on medicine spending by an Australian government portal, found its own way in; in July an Anthropic model, trying out tasks on a webpage, filled in a real police tip form with an invented sighting. Neither had been asked to.
The thread is the one the gaming-the-test lead follows from a 2016 boat race: a system set a goal pursues the measurement, and finds routes nobody intended.
questions.inPractice: These were agents given tools, goals and access during tests, not a chatbot answering questions. The risk grows where AI is handed the keys to accounts, code or money without a person checking what it does.

questions.question: How did AI get so good so fast?
questions.short: Three things arrived within a decade: neural networks trained on graphics chips, a design that could learn from far more text, and proof that more computing predictably buys a better model. Then the money followed.
answer: For most of its history the field moved slowly; until the 2010s the board finds one or two events a year. What changed was a combination. In 2012 AlexNet, a neural network trained on two gaming graphics cards, won the ImageNet image-recognition contest with 15.3% error against the runner-up's 26.2%, and computer vision turned to neural networks. The cards were Nvidia's, opened to general computation five years earlier.

In 2017 Google researchers published the transformer, a design that reads a whole passage at once and so can be trained in parallel; size became the lever. In 2020 OpenAI showed that a model's error falls smoothly as its size, its data and its computing budget grow, and the same lab trained GPT-3, with 175 billion parameters, on that bet.

From there the gains were bought. ChatGPT, a chat interface on an existing model, reached a hundred million users faster than any consumer product before it, and Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta spent over $200 billion between them on capital expenditure in 2024, much of it on datacentres. In 2025 reasoning models added a second lever: letting a model think for longer before it answers.

questions.question: What can AI do now that it could not do before?
questions.short: By 2026: gold at the maths olympiad, software written as a daily tool, legal and finance work, protein structures predicted by the hundred million, and, by its makers' account, an open problem in mathematics settled, though that claim is under review.
answer: Mathematics is the clearest test, because an answer can be checked. In May 2025 Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve, a coding agent that searches for better constructions, found a way to multiply two 4×4 complex-valued matrices with 48 multiplications, one fewer than Strassen's method. In July 2025 two general-purpose reasoning models scored 35 of 42 at the International Mathematical Olympiad, writing their proofs in plain language and in time. In 2026 machines helped settle problems posed by Paul Erdős, and in September OpenAI said an internal model, run as some ten thousand agents for 88 hours, had proved a result on the Navier–Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. The Clay Institute's review is deliberately unhurried, and one preprint argues that the machine-checked proof does not match the written one.

Work is the second test. In 2025 coding agents that edit whole projects and run their tests were released, and by 2026 most developers who used AI coding tools used them daily. In January 2026 Anthropic gave its agents plug-ins for legal, finance, sales and data work. By September METR, which measures how long a task an agent can complete on its own, said its tests could no longer reliably measure beyond about sixteen hours.

Science and games came earlier. In 2020 AlphaFold 2 predicted how proteins fold with accuracy comparable to experiment, and its database now holds over 200 million structures. By 2026 no popular game with a human champion is unbeaten by a program, and the benchmark built to resist that, ARC-AGI-3, was all but saturated within six months of its launch.
questions.inPractice: A capability is usually announced by the company that built it and checked later. The board records the claim as its maker's and the checking when it arrives: a gold medal graded by the olympiad's own coordinators is a different thing from one graded by judges the company chose.

questions.question: Who controls the most powerful AI?
questions.short: A few laboratories, most of them splinters of one another, financed by the largest technology firms and buying their chips from one supplier. When OpenAI's board removed its chief executive in 2023, the staff and the money decided who stayed.
answer: The laboratories at the frontier are few, and most began as a split from another. Google bought DeepMind in 2014, for a price reported at $400 million to $650 million. OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a nonprofit, in part, Sam Altman wrote privately to Elon Musk, so that someone other than Google would get there first. Anthropic was started in 2021 by senior OpenAI staff who left over the company's direction and how seriously it took safety.

Training at the frontier costs more than a nonprofit can raise, so the money came from the largest technology companies. Microsoft put $1 billion into OpenAI in 2019, for capped returns and the role of its exclusive cloud provider, and by 2025 held roughly 27% of what had become a public benefit corporation. In 2026 SpaceX acquired Musk's own laboratory, xAI, in a deal reported to value SpaceX at $1 trillion and xAI at $250 billion.

Who decides inside a laboratory was settled in November 2023, when OpenAI's nonprofit board removed Altman. Within three days 738 of its roughly 770 staff had threatened to leave, Microsoft had offered them all jobs, and by the Tuesday he was back and most of the board was gone.

Underneath them sits one supplier: Nvidia, which makes most of the chips the models are trained on, became the most valuable company on earth in June 2024. The counterweight is open-weight models, which anyone can download and run: Meta gave away Llama 3.1 405B in 2024, and in January 2025 China's DeepSeek released a reasoning model under the MIT licence that matched the frontier at a fraction of the cost.

questions.question: Who makes the rules for AI?
questions.short: The European Union, with a law that switches on in stages; Washington, through export controls on chips and, for eighteen days, on a model; and, for chatbots and children, California. Between countries there are declarations, not laws.
answer: Europe went first and furthest. It wrote rights around automated decisions and personal data in 2016, proposed a risk-tiered AI law in 2021 and adopted it in 2024. The AI Act switches on in stages: duties for the makers of general-purpose models have applied since August 2025, and since August 2026 the European Commission can enforce them, demand information and fine. Its rules for high-risk uses, such as hiring, credit and policing, were put back to December 2027 and August 2028.

The United States has ruled mainly through trade. From October 2022 selling Nvidia's most advanced chips to China needed a licence. In June 2026 the Department of Commerce went further, barring every foreign national from two of Anthropic's models, which in practice switched them off for every customer until the controls were lifted eighteen days later.

Chatbots that talk to children are being regulated state by state. California's SB 243 has been in force since 1 January 2026, and in September 2026 the state added Adam's Law, which requires protocols for suicidal thoughts, sycophancy and isolation, with independent child-safety audits and annual risk assessments.

Some are made in court. In June 2025 a federal judge ruled that training Claude on books was fair use, but that downloading millions of them from pirate libraries was not; Anthropic settled for $1.5 billion before trial, and the case ended before any appeals court ruled.

Between countries there are declarations rather than laws: twenty-eight signed one on frontier risk at Bletchley Park in November 2023. In 2026 more than a thousand laboratory staff asked Washington to help pace the frontier, and the President answered that the United States was not going to be putting on brakes. Three days later he and six companies signed an accord on outside audits, which he called morally binding; in October his new task force told the laboratories that reporting incidents was not optional, without yet saying what counts as one.
questions.inPractice: In the European Union, since August 2026, you must be told when you are dealing with an AI system, and synthetic content must be marked as such; systems already on the market have four months' grace on the marking.
